Period schedule:

Total: 7 periods · 5h 15min

periods.activity_title: Cross-Products, Cooking Ratios, and Map Scales

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Map Making Activity, p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make a sketch of their classroom at scale 1:50, marking locations of teacher's desk, blackboard, fans, lights, and other objects using appropriate symbols.

time_bands.activity: Open with the idli-batter scenario from section 3.1: Viswanath uses 6 cups rice and 3 cups urad dal; Puneet uses 4 cups and 2 cups. Students write both ratios and test the cross-product rule (a×d = b×c) to confirm proportionality, articulating in their own words what it means for two ratios to be 'the same' in a proportional relationship.

Introduce the Representative Fraction (RF) concept from section 3.2: RF 1:60,00,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 60 km on the ground. Students practise converting a set of map distances to ground distances and reverse, using the RF as a multiplier, working in pairs and sharing reasoning.

Map Making Activity, p.57 ("Students make a sketch of their classroom at scale 1:50, marking locations...."). Students measure actual classroom dimensions and furniture positions with a ruler or metre tape, scale each measurement by 1:50, and draw the floor plan on graph paper with appropriate symbols.

Pairs share one conversion they found tricky during the map sketch. The class verifies the cross-product check (a×d = b×c) on one real measurement from the activity to confirm the scale was applied correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: The cross-product equality (a×d = b×c) established in section 3.1 is the anchor that makes every map-scale calculation trustworthy — watch for students who invert the RF and multiply instead of dividing. A common slip is treating 1 cm = 60,00,000 cm as 60 km and then mixing centimetres and kilometres mid-calculation; prompt students to convert units before applying the RF.

periods.activity_title: Spice Mix to Paint: Multi-Term Ratio Rules

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 3.3 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Purple paint mixed in ratio Red:Blue:White :: 2:3:5; given 10 litres of white, find litres of red and blue.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 3.3 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cement concrete ratio 1:1.5:3; given 3 bags of cement, find total bags of concrete mixture.

time_bands.activity: Present the four-ingredient spice mix from section 3.3: coriander:chillies:dal:fenugreek :: 8:4:2:1. Ask students to double and then halve the recipe, recording their scaled quantities. Students articulate the general observation that every term is multiplied by the same factor, leading them to state the proportionality rule a/p = b/q = c/r = d/s in their own words.

Walk through Example 1, section 3.3 p.58 ("Purple paint mixed in ratio Red:Blue:White :: 2:3:5; given 10 litres of white...."). Students first estimate the red and blue quantities by reasoning about the ratio, then verify their estimate against the proportional calculation, discussing why the 'anchor term' (the known quantity) controls all others.

Walk through Example 2, section 3.3 p.58 ("Cement concrete ratio 1:1.5:3; given 3 bags of cement, find total bags...."). Students set up the proportional chain, handle the decimal ratio term 1.5 by converting to whole-number form (2:3:6 scaled), compute the total, and compare both solution paths to assess efficiency.

Students pose a new three-term ratio problem from a context of their choice (cooking, craft, construction) and exchange it with a neighbour to solve, reinforcing the multi-term proportionality rule through problem-posing.

periods.teacher_notes: The general rule a/p = b/q = c/r = d/s is the conceptual core here — students who treat multi-term ratios as a series of separate two-term ratios often lose the multiplicative link between all terms. Watch for errors when ratio terms are decimals or fractions; encourage students to scale to whole-number equivalents before computing.

textbook_segments.title: Dividing a Whole in a Given Ratio

periods.activity_title: Dividing Totals: Concrete, Paint, and Triangle Angles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 3.4 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: 110 units of concrete needed in ratio 1:1.5:3; find units of cement, sand, and gravel.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 3.4 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: 50 ml of purple paint in ratio 2:3:5; find ml of red, blue, and white paint.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 3.4 p.60
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a triangle with angles in ratio 1:3:5; compute each angle using angle-sum = 180°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cricket practice session 150 min in ratio warm-up:batting:bowling:fielding :: 3:4:3:5; find time for each activity.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.4 p.60
textbook_items_in_class.description: Library books Odiya:Hindi:English :: 3:2:1; given 288 Odiya books, find Hindi and English counts.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 3.4 p.60
homework.description: 100 coins in ratio ₹10:₹5:₹2:₹1 :: 4:3:2:1; find total monetary value.

time_bands.activity: State the division formula explicitly: each part = total × (its ratio term) ÷ (sum of all ratio terms). Students copy and annotate the formula, labelling each variable with a word description before any numbers are used.

Work through Example 3, section 3.4 p.59 ("110 units of concrete needed in ratio 1:1.5:3; find units of cement, sand, and gravel."). Students compute the sum of ratio terms, apply the formula to each component, and verify by confirming the three parts add back to 110.

Students independently attempt Example 4, section 3.4 p.59 ("50 ml of purple paint in ratio 2:3:5; find ml of red, blue, and white paint.") before the class consolidates. Then Example 5, section 3.4 p.60 ("Construct a triangle with angles in ratio 1:3:5; compute each angle using angle-sum = 180°.") is discussed: students identify the angle-sum constraint as the 'total' in the formula.

Pairs attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60 ("Cricket practice session 150 min in ratio warm-up:batting:bowling:fielding :: 3:4:3:5....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 3.4 p.60 ("Library books Odiya:Hindi:English :: 3:2:1; given 288 Odiya books...."), practising the division algorithm in different real-world settings.

Students articulate one situation from daily life where they might divide a total in a given ratio, and explain how the formula would apply. Figure it Out Q3, section 3.4 p.60 ("100 coins in ratio ₹10:₹5:₹2:₹1 :: 4:3:2:1; find total monetary value.") is set for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error is dividing the total by one ratio term instead of the sum of all terms — a quick additive check (do the parts sum to the whole?) catches this immediately. Example 5 is a valuable moment to connect proportional division with geometry: the angle-sum constraint plays exactly the role that '110 units' plays in Example 3. For students who finish early, Example 5 (section 3.4 p.60) offers a geometric extension.

periods.activity_title: From Ratio to Sector: Building a Pie Chart Step by Step

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.5 p.62
textbook_items_in_class.description: 360 people vote on favourite season (90 summer, 120 rainy, rest winter); draw pie chart.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.5 p.62
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw pie chart from TV channel preference data: Entertainment 50%, Sports 25%, News 15%, Information 10%.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 3.5 p.62
homework.description: Survey classmates on favourite subject; record data in table across 7 subjects and construct pie chart.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the grade-distribution example from section 3.5: grades A:B:C:D:E :: 12:10:8:6:4. Students use the HCF method to reduce this to simplest form (6:5:4:3:2) and state the sum of terms, establishing that 360° is the 'whole' that will be divided.

Students apply the ratio-division formula (established in section 3.4) to compute the five sector angles (108°, 90°, 72°, 54°, 36°), verify the sum equals 360°, then follow the step-by-step construction procedure from section 3.5: draw a circle, mark one radius, measure successive angles with a protractor, and label each sector.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.5 p.62 ("360 people vote on favourite season (90 summer, 120 rainy, rest winter); draw pie chart."). Students identify the number of 'winter' voters, convert each count to a sector angle by forming the ratio over 360, and construct the pie chart.

Figure it Out Q2, section 3.5 p.62 ("Draw pie chart from TV channel preference data: Entertainment 50%, Sports 25%, News 15%, Information 10%."). Students convert percentages to angles (percentage × 3.6°), noting this as a special case of proportional division where the total is 100%.

Introduce Figure it Out Q3, section 3.5 p.62 ("Survey classmates on favourite subject; record data in table across 7 subjects and construct pie chart.") as a home task requiring students to collect their own data and complete the construction.

periods.teacher_notes: The proportional division of 360° is a direct application of section 3.4's division algorithm — students who understood the concrete examples there should transfer the method readily. A common error is computing sector angles without reducing to simplest form first, which still gives the same angle but can mislead students about whether simplification is required; discuss both routes. The self-survey in Figure it Out Q3 (section 3.5 p.62) makes the data personally meaningful.

periods.activity_title: Constant Product, Contrasting Patterns: Building the xy = k Rule

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.6 p.65
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify which of three x-y tables shows inverse proportion by checking whether xy is constant. (Three sub-tables: (i) not inverse, (ii) direct proportion, (iii) inverse proportion.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.6 p.65
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill empty cells in an inverse proportion table (x: 16, 12, ?, 36; y: 9, ?, 48, ?).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 3.6 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Motorcycle at 30 km/h takes 3 hours Lucknow–Kanpur; introduces speed-time table to show inverse relationship, leading to the xy=k definition.

time_bands.activity: Present the speed-time table from section 3.6 (walk 5 km/h×18h, bicycle 15×6, motorcycle 30×3, car 60×1.5). Students compute the product for each row, record the pattern, and conjecture: 'When one quantity doubles, the other halves; their product stays constant.' Students articulate how this differs from direct proportion, where the quotient is constant.

Walk through Example 2, section 3.6 p.63 ("Motorcycle at 30 km/h takes 3 hours Lucknow–Kanpur; introduces speed-time table to show inverse relationship, leading to the xy=k definition."). Students derive the formal rule x₁y₁ = x₂y₂ from their observed pattern and write a one-sentence justification of why xy must remain constant.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.6 p.65 ("Identify which of three x-y tables shows inverse proportion by checking whether xy is constant."). Students test all three sub-tables, categorising each and explaining their classification in writing — 'this table shows direct proportion because the quotient x/y is constant, not the product.'

Figure it Out Q2, section 3.6 p.65 ("Fill empty cells in an inverse proportion table (x: 16, 12, ?, 36; y: 9, ?, 48, ?)."). Students use xy = k (where k is computed from the first known pair) to fill the missing values, verifying each completed pair against the constant product.
Students write a brief comparison — direct proportion has constant quotient, inverse proportion has constant product — and share one original example of each from daily life.

periods.teacher_notes: The contrast between constant quotient (direct) and constant product (inverse) is the conceptual hinge of section 3.6 — press students to articulate both criteria in their own words before moving to calculation. A common confusion is applying the direct-proportion cross-multiplication rule to inverse problems; Figure it Out Q1's classification task is a targeted correction for this. For additional self-study, Example 1, section 3.6 p.63 ("5 workers move 4500 bricks in a day....") offers a direct-proportion contrast problem students can attempt independently.

periods.activity_title: Workers, Pumps, Provisions: Applying x₁y₁ = x₂y₂

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 3.6 p.65
textbook_items_in_class.description: 20 workers complete road in 4 days; find days needed for 10 workers using x₁y₁ = x₂y₂.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 3.6 p.66
textbook_items_in_class.description: 2 pumps fill tank in 18 hours; find time for 4 pumps using inverse proportion.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 3.6 p.66
textbook_items_in_class.description: Food provisions for 80 students for 15 days; 20 more students join — find how many days provisions last.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.6 p.67
textbook_items_in_class.description: Classify six real-world quantity pairs as inverse proportion or not (taps-time, painters-days, distance-petrol, cyclist speed-time, cloth length-price, pages-reading time).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.6 p.68
textbook_items_in_class.description: 3 workers paint fence in 4 days; one more worker joins — find days to finish; state assumptions.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 3.6 p.67
homework.description: Tank water sufficient for 20 families for 6 days; 10 more families move in — find how long water lasts; state assumptions (Math Talk).

time_bands.activity: Students articulate the inverse proportion rule xy = k and write the working equation x₁y₁ = x₂y₂, identifying what x and y represent in a workers-and-days context before any numerical values are substituted.

Walk through Example 3, section 3.6 p.65 ("20 workers complete road in 4 days; find days needed for 10 workers....") and Example 4, section 3.6 p.66 ("2 pumps fill tank in 18 hours; find time for 4 pumps...."). After each, students verify by checking x₁y₁ = x₂y₂ with their computed answer, building the habit of checking the constant product.

Work through Example 5, section 3.6 p.66 ("Food provisions for 80 students for 15 days; 20 more students join — find how many days provisions last."). Students discuss why increasing the number of students decreases the number of days, connecting the direction of change to the inverse relationship.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.6 p.67 ("Classify six real-world quantity pairs as inverse proportion or not....") in pairs: students must justify each classification with a reason, not just a label. Then Figure it Out Q6, section 3.6 p.68 ("3 workers paint fence in 4 days; one more worker joins — find days to finish; state assumptions.") as an independent attempt.

Brief whole-class consolidation: students report one pair from Figure it Out Q1 that surprised them and explain why the relationship is or is not inverse. Figure it Out Q3, section 3.6 p.67 ("Tank water sufficient for 20 families for 6 days; 10 more families move in — find how long water lasts; state assumptions.") is set for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The worked examples here span workers-days, pumps-hours, and provisions-people — all structurally identical uses of x₁y₁ = x₂y₂, so students should quickly see the pattern and set up equations independently. Watch for students who multiply both quantities in the same direction (treating it as direct); the classification task in Figure it Out Q1 (section 3.6 p.67) is designed to surface this confusion. For confident students, Example 6, section 3.6 p.66 ("Ram and Shyam cutting vegetables....") extends into unit-work-rate reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Extended Inverse Problems: Chairs, Tanks, Machines, and Combined Work

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.6 p.68
textbook_items_in_class.description: 25 rows × 12 chairs per row; rearrange with 20 chairs per row — find new number of rows.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 3.6 p.68
textbook_items_in_class.description: 8 periods × 45 minutes; find period duration if school has 9 periods (total school hours unchanged).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.6 p.68
textbook_items_in_class.description: Small pump fills tank in 3 hours, large pump in 2 hours; find time if both work together.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 3.6 p.68
textbook_items_in_class.description: 42 machines produce toys in 63 days; find machines needed to produce same number in 54 days.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 3.6 p.66
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ram cuts vegetables in 1 hour, Shyam in 1.5 hours; find combined time using unit-work rates and direct proportion.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 3.6 p.68
homework.description: Car at 60 km/h reaches destination in 2 hours; find time at 80 km/h.

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q8, section 3.6 p.68 ("25 rows × 12 chairs per row; rearrange with 20 chairs per row — find new number of rows.") and Figure it Out Q9, section 3.6 p.68 ("8 periods × 45 minutes; find period duration if school has 9 periods...."). After solving, pairs explain to each other why the constant product (total chairs; total minutes) defines the inverse relationship in each case.

Introduce unit-work-rate reasoning via Example 6, section 3.6 p.66 ("Ram cuts vegetables in 1 hour, Shyam in 1.5 hours; find combined time using unit-work rates and direct proportion."). Students compute each person's fraction of work done per unit time, add the rates, and use the combined rate to find the total time — recognising this as a bridge between inverse and direct proportionality.

Students independently attempt Figure it Out Q10, section 3.6 p.68 ("Small pump fills tank in 3 hours, large pump in 2 hours; find time if both work together.") using the unit-work-rate method just established, then check by verifying the combined rate makes intuitive sense (answer should be less than 2 hours).

Figure it Out Q11, section 3.6 p.68 ("42 machines produce toys in 63 days; find machines needed to produce same number in 54 days.") as a quick application of x₁y₁ = x₂y₂. Students set up and solve, noting the direction of change as a self-check.

Students reflect: name one real-world pair they encountered today that uses inverse proportion and write the constant product for it. Figure it Out Q12, section 3.6 p.68 ("Car at 60 km/h reaches destination in 2 hours; find time at 80 km/h.") is set for home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The unit-work-rate method in Example 6 (section 3.6 p.66) is the most conceptually demanding step in this unit — students often try to average the two times rather than add rates. Emphasise that fractions of work per unit time add (direct proportion), while numbers of workers and time taken multiply to a constant (inverse proportion). Figure it Out Q12 (section 3.6 p.68) is a straightforward speed-time inverse problem that consolidates the chapter's closing theme.

items.prompt: Two paint mixtures are being compared: Mixture P uses 6 parts red and 9 parts blue; Mixture Q uses 4 parts red and 6 parts blue. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between these two mixtures?

options.label: A
options.text: The mixtures are not proportional because the ratio 6:9 cannot be simplified.

options.label: B
options.text: The mixtures are not proportional because they use different quantities.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The mixtures are proportional. Cross-product check: 6 × 6 = 36 and 9 × 4 = 36; since both cross-products are equal, the ratios 6:9 and 4:6 are equivalent (both simplify to 2:3).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the cross-product rule: a×d = b×c confirms two ratios are proportional.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses proportionality with equality of quantities, not recognising that different amounts can maintain the same ratio.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student attempts an additive comparison rather than a multiplicative (cross-product) test.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly believes a ratio that can be simplified is not proportional to another ratio.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the idli-batter example in section 3.1 and re-read how the cross-product rule is stated.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a second pair of ratios that are proportional to 6:9, and verify using both the cross-product and the simplified form.

exercise.description: Students make a sketch of their classroom at scale 1:50, marking locations of teacher's desk, blackboard, fans, lights, and other objects using appropriate symbols.

items.prompt: A spice mix is prepared in the ratio coriander : chillies : dal : fenugreek = 8 : 4 : 2 : 1. If a batch is scaled so that the fenugreek quantity doubles, which of the following correctly states the new ratio?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When fenugreek doubles from 1 to 2, every other term must also double to maintain proportionality. The new ratio is 16:8:4:2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a multi-term proportional ratio, all terms scale by the same factor: a/p = b/q = c/r = d/s.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student changed only the fenugreek term, not recognising that all terms must scale by the same factor.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added a fixed number to each term rather than multiplying by the scale factor.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student doubled only one of the middle terms, showing partial application of the scaling rule.

inclusivity.support: Return to the spice mix example in section 3.3 and re-read the explanation of why all terms must use the same scale factor.
inclusivity.challenge: Write your own three-ingredient recipe in a ratio, then describe what happens to the ratio when the batch size is tripled — is the simplified ratio the same or different?

exercise.description: Purple paint mixed in ratio Red:Blue:White :: 2:3:5; given 10 litres of white, find litres of red and blue.

items.prompt: A student says: 'If 6 taps take 4 hours to fill a tank, then 3 taps will take 2 hours — because when the number of taps halves, the time halves too.' Identify the error in this reasoning and explain the correct relationship between the number of taps and the time taken.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student has applied direct proportion incorrectly. Fewer taps mean more time is needed, not less — this is an inverse proportion. The correct reasoning is: 6 × 4 = 24 (constant product), so 3 taps take 24 ÷ 3 = 8 hours.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that taps and time form an inverse proportion (xy = k), so halving the taps doubles the time.

inclusivity.support: Talk through the problem with a partner first: if you reduce the number of taps, does filling get faster or slower? Then use x₁y₁ = x₂y₂.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the problem so that a third pump is added instead of removed, and re-explain using the same inverse-proportion reasoning.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.6 p.65
exercise.description: Identify which of three x-y tables shows inverse proportion by checking whether xy is constant. (Three sub-tables: (i) not inverse, (ii) direct proportion, (iii) inverse proportion.)

items.prompt: A map has a Representative Fraction of 1 : 50,00,000. On this map, the distance between two towns is 3.4 cm. (a) Calculate the actual distance between the towns in kilometres. (b) If another pair of towns is actually 170 km apart, find their distance on the map in centimetres. Show your working clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Actual distance = 3.4 × 50,00,000 cm = 1,70,00,000 cm = 170 km. (b) Map distance = 170 km ÷ 50 km per cm = 3.4 cm. (Since RF 1:50,00,000 means 1 cm = 50 km, map distance = 170 ÷ 50 = 3.4 cm.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply map distance by the RF denominator (in matching units) to get actual distance; divide actual distance by the RF denominator to get map distance.

inclusivity.support: Draw a small table with two columns — map distance and actual distance — and write the RF as the first row (1 cm = 50 km) to see the proportional structure.
inclusivity.challenge: If the same map were redrawn at RF 1:25,00,000, what would both distances become on the new map?

exercise.description: Students make a sketch of their classroom at scale 1:50, marking locations of teacher's desk, blackboard, fans, lights, and other objects using appropriate symbols.

items.section_title: Dividing a Whole in a Given Ratio
items.prompt: A 180-minute study session is divided among three subjects in the ratio Mathematics : Science : English = 4 : 3 : 2. (a) Find the number of minutes allocated to each subject. (b) Verify your answer by checking that the three amounts sum to 180 minutes. Show all working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sum of ratio terms = 4 + 3 + 2 = 9. Mathematics = 180 × 4/9 = 80 min; Science = 180 × 3/9 = 60 min; English = 180 × 2/9 = 40 min. Verification: 80 + 60 + 40 = 180. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total by the sum of ratio terms, then multiply each term by this unit value.

inclusivity.support: Use a number line or bar diagram to represent 180 minutes, then shade sections proportional to 4, 3, and 2 before calculating.
inclusivity.challenge: If Mathematics time increases by 10 minutes and the total stays at 180, suggest a new ratio for all three subjects and check whether it can be expressed in whole numbers.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60
exercise.description: Cricket practice session 150 min in ratio warm-up:batting:bowling:fielding :: 3:4:3:5; find time for each activity.

items.prompt: A survey of 200 students asked about their preferred mode of transport to school. The results were: Bicycle 60, Walk 50, Bus 40, Two-wheeler 30, Car 20. (a) Reduce the counts to their simplest ratio. (b) Calculate the sector angle (in degrees) for each category. (c) Verify that the five angles sum to 360°. Show all working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the HCF to simplify the ratio, then apply the proportional division formula with 360° as the total.

inclusivity.support: First convert each count to a fraction of the total 200 students, then multiply each fraction by 360° to get the sector angle.
inclusivity.challenge: If the 'Car' category were merged with 'Two-wheeler', describe how the pie chart changes and recalculate only the affected sectors.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.5 p.62
exercise.description: 360 people vote on favourite season (90 summer, 120 rainy, rest winter); draw pie chart.

items.prompt: An auditorium has 30 rows with 18 chairs per row. The chairs are to be rearranged so that each row has 27 chairs, keeping the total number of chairs the same. Find the new number of rows. Show your working using the inverse proportion rule.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total chairs = 30 × 18 = 540. Using x₁y₁ = x₂y₂: 30 × 18 = x₂ × 27. x₂ = 540 ÷ 27 = 20 rows.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply x₁y₁ = x₂y₂: the product of rows and chairs per row is constant (total chairs).

inclusivity.support: First count the total chairs (30 × 18), then ask: how many groups of 27 fit in that total?
inclusivity.challenge: If the auditorium is further rearranged to 36 chairs per row, find the number of rows and explain the pattern you observe as chairs per row increases.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.6 p.68
exercise.description: 25 rows × 12 chairs per row; rearrange with 20 chairs per row — find new number of rows.

items.prompt: Pipe A fills a water tank completely in 4 hours. Pipe B fills the same tank completely in 6 hours. If both pipes are opened at the same time, how long will it take to fill the tank? Show your working using unit-work rates.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Pipe A fills 1/4 of the tank per hour; Pipe B fills 1/6 of the tank per hour. Combined rate = 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12 of the tank per hour. Time to fill = 1 ÷ (5/12) = 12/5 = 2.4 hours = 2 hours 24 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find each pipe's unit work rate (fraction of tank per hour), add the rates, then take the reciprocal for combined time.

inclusivity.support: Draw a bar representing the whole tank, shade 1/4 for what Pipe A does in one hour and 1/6 for what Pipe B does, then count how many such combined portions fill the bar.
inclusivity.challenge: A third pipe drains the tank in 12 hours while A and B fill it. Find the time to fill the tank with all three pipes open.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.6 p.68
exercise.description: Small pump fills tank in 3 hours, large pump in 2 hours; find time if both work together.
